title: Gudeg, and the many lives of -nya
goal: Talk about food the way Indonesians do — its taste, its colour, its price, its secret — and get fully comfortable with *-nya*, the busiest suffix in the language: "the", "his/her/its", the maker of nouns, the exclamation, and the little sentence-openers *katanya, sepertinya, rupanya, tampaknya*.
bekal: use *-nya* for "the" and "its", and to turn adjectives and verbs into nouns: *rasanya*, *pedasnya*, *masaknya*

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Masak gudeg
dialogs.intro: A Saturday morning in April, in Bu Endang's kitchen next door. A big clay pot, a pile of young jackfruit, and a bundle of leaves Sarah does not recognise. Bu Endang has promised to teach her gudeg, Yogyakarta's signature dish.

notes: **Gudeg** is young jackfruit (*nangka muda*, in Yogya also *gori*) simmered for hours in coconut milk, palm sugar and spices until it turns sweet, soft and dark. It is served with rice, chicken, egg, tofu and a fiery side of *krecek*. "Gudeg" and "Jogja" are more or less the same word in the minds of most Indonesians.

**Pantesan** — "no wonder" — is the spoken form of *pantas saja*. You will hear it every time someone finally understands why: *Pantesan macet, ada kecelakaan* (no wonder it's jammed, there's been an accident). 💬 In writing: *pantas saja* or *pantaslah*.

**Kemanisan** — "too sweet". *Ke- + adjective + -an* in everyday speech means "too much of it": *kemahalan* (too expensive), *kepedasan* (too spicy), *kebesaran* (too big — of clothes). B1 returns to it; for now just enjoy using it to complain.

**Kata teman saya** — "my friend says". *Kata* + person is how Indonesian reports who said something, with no verb: *Kata dokter, saya harus istirahat*. When you do not name the source, it becomes *katanya* (Unit 14 and below).

**Coba cicipi** — "have a taste". *Cicip* is to taste a small amount; *cicipi* adds the *-i* of doing something to a target (Unit 6). *Coba* in front softens it from an order into an invitation, as it did in Unit 14.

**Makin lama makin enak** — "the longer, the tastier". The pattern *makin X makin Y* (formal *semakin … semakin …*) is the Indonesian "the more …, the more …": *Makin malam makin ramai*. And Bu Endang's closing proverb, *alon-alon waton kelakon*, is Javanese for "slowly, as long as it gets there" — practically Yogyakarta's motto. *Kayak* is spoken for *seperti*.

grammars.title: -nya as "the" and "his / her / its"
body: You met this in A1. The key point at A2: *-nya* is used far more often than English "the", every time a thing is already known to both speakers — because it is in front of you, or it belongs to something already mentioned.

head: Indonesian
Word for word
English
Which *-nya*
rows: the one in front of us

after: A useful test: if you could say "its" or "the … of it" in English, Indonesian very probably wants *-nya*. *Bagaimana rasanya?* is not "how is taste?" but "how is the taste of it?"

⚠️ *-nya* does not replace *itu*. *Nangkanya* is "the jackfruit (we both know)"; *nangka itu* is "that jackfruit (there, not this one)". Mixing them up is rarely confusing, but using *itu* everywhere sounds like you are pointing at things.

grammars.title: -nya turns words into nouns
body: Add *-nya* to an adjective or a verb and it becomes a noun: "the sweetness of it", "the cooking of it". English needs a new word; Indonesian just adds the suffix.

head: Base
With -nya
Example
English
rows: The sweetness comes from palm sugar.
How far is it, in kilometres?

after: This is why *Berapa harganya?* and *Berapa jauhnya?* sound so natural: you are asking about "the price of it", "the distance of it".

💬 In speech the noun made with *-nya* often goes first, as the topic, and the comment follows: *Masaknya lama. Rasanya enak. Harganya lumayan.* Three sentences, three topics, no verb "to be" in sight.

⚠️ Do not stack it on a word that already has a possessor: *rasa gudeg ini* (the taste of this gudeg) needs no *-nya*, but *rasanya* on its own does the same job once everyone knows which gudeg you mean.

dialogs.title: Second dialogue — Review gudeg Eyang
dialogs.intro: The next morning. Dimas has borrowed his grandmother's phone to film a video for his (very small) channel, the gudeg has had its night to rest, and Sarah has been recruited as the guest taster. Bu Endang watches from the doorway.

notes: **Enaknya! Pedasnya!** — the exclamation *-nya*: adjective + *-nya*, said with feeling, means "how …!" or "it's so …!". Add the thing if you like: *Pedasnya sambal ini!* (this sambal is so hot!). It is warmer and more spontaneous than *enak sekali*.

**Eyang** is the respectful Javanese word for grandparent, used by families who like a bit of formality; *Eyang putri* is grandmother, *Eyang kakung* grandfather. Many families shorten them to *Uti* and *Kakung*, while others say *Mbah*. All of them are fine; follow what the family uses.
**Krecek** is crispy cow skin cooked in a spicy coconut stew, the red-hot partner to sweet gudeg. Sarah's reaction is the correct one.

**Bikin nagih** — "makes you want more", addictive, of food. *Nagih* comes from *tagih* (to demand payment): the food keeps sending you the bill. 💬 *Bikin* is the everyday word for *membuat* (make) in both senses: *bikin kue* (make a cake), *bikin capek* (make you tired).

**Nyala** — "on, lit" — is the spoken form of *menyala*. *Lampunya nyala* (the light's on), *HP-ku nggak mau nyala* (my phone won't turn on). The verb for switching something on is *menyalakan* (Unit 5).

**Review, like, subscribe.** Indonesian children speak fluent video-platform English, and nobody bothers to translate it. You will hear *nge-review*, *di-like*, *subscribe* with Indonesian prefixes glued on. *Dadah* is how children (and adults talking to children) say bye-bye.

grammars.title: Sentence openers with -nya
body: A family of *-nya* words sits at the front of a sentence and tells the listener how you know or how sure you are. They are among the most frequent words in spoken Indonesian.
after: *Rupanya* reports a discovery ("so it turns out"), *sepertinya* a guess ("I think"), *katanya* someone else's word ("I heard"). Choosing the right one makes you sound careful rather than blunt.

💬 *Kayaknya* is the everyday form of *sepertinya* and you will hear it constantly: *Kayaknya mau hujan*. *Tampaknya* belongs to news and reports. Two more members of the family: *untungnya* (luckily) and *sebenarnya* (actually).

blocks.text: Here is *-nya* in one table. When you meet it in a sentence, run down the list; the context will always pick one.

head: Job
Example
English

It turns out she's gone home.
object "it / him / her" after a verb

blocks.text: ⚠️ The last two are written Indonesian. In speech people say *Udah saya baca* or *Saya udah baca itu*, and *sama dia*, *buat dia* rather than *dengannya* and *untuknya*.

blocks.title: Exclaiming like a local
items: *Mahalnya!* — How expensive! (at the market, quietly, before you start bargaining)
*Cantiknya batik ini!* — What a beautiful batik! The thing follows the adjective.
*Aduh, panasnya!* — Phew, it's so hot! *Aduh* and *wah* are the natural launch words.
*Lucunya!* — How cute! Said about every baby and every kitten in Indonesia.
⚠️ Tone matters: *Lamanya!* with a sigh is a complaint ("how long this is taking!"), with a smile it is wonder.

blocks.text: Indonesian has a precise vocabulary for taste and texture, and people use it: a *warung* conversation about whether today's soup is *gurih* enough is entirely normal.

blocks.title: Compliments and complaints
items: *Enak banget! Bumbunya meresap.* — Delicious! The spices have really soaked in.
*Pas, nggak kemanisan.* — Just right, not too sweet.
*Agak keasinan, ya.* — A bit too salty, isn't it. (*agak* softens it)
*Nagih!* — Addictive! The highest praise a snack can get.
